content.title: About
content.content: Ground raw beef is finely minced raw beef obtained from various cuts of the carcass. It has a bright red color, soft texture, and a neutral flavor that readily absorbs seasonings and sauces during cooking. Ground beef is commonly used for patties, meatballs, sauces, fillings, and quick‑cook dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ground beef can be made from both lean and fattier cuts, giving a range of fat percentages.
In the United States the minimum lean‑to‑fat ratio for ground beef is usually 90 % lean (10 % fat), while other countries may sell higher‑fat blends.
Ground beef is favored for dishes that require fast, even cooking, such as chili, tacos, and lasagna.
Raw meat products can harbor pathogens, making proper handling and storage essential.
In some cuisines raw minced beef is served as steak tartare, seasoned with herbs, spices, and sauces.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Ground beef provides complete animal protein that supports muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 in beef is essential for nerve function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune health and wound healing.

items.title: Provides creatine and carnitine
items.content: These compounds aid muscle energy metabolism and may improve physical performance.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Raw ground beef can contain Salmonella, E. coli and other pathogens; keep it at ≤ 4 °C and cook to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Higher‑fat ground beef can contribute to elevated cholesterol if consumed frequently.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions of undercooked ground beef may cause stomach upset.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ground beef is typically cooked: sautéed, browned, baked, or simmered. Use it for burgers, meatballs, sauces, stuffed peppers, casseroles, and more. Ensure thorough cooking to eliminate harmful bacteria.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ground beef in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 1‑2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C; it retains quality for 3‑4 months. Thaw frozen beef in the fridge, not at room temperature, before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Ribeye steak is a cut from the beef rib section, known for its marbled fat and rich flavor. The meat is tender, juicy, and suitable for quick searing or slow cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name "ribeye" comes from the eye‑shaped fat deposit in the rib area.
Marbling (intramuscular fat) is responsible for the steak’s juiciness and flavor.
Traditionally ribeye is grilled or pan‑seared in a hot cast‑iron skillet.
In the United States ribeye is one of the most popular cuts in steakhouses.
Ribeye quality is graded by USDA (Prime, Choice, Select) based on marbling.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron and zinc
items.content: The iron in beef is highly bioavailable, and zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ribeye supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: Marbled fat contains monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that, in moderation, can support heart health.

items.title: Creatine source
items.content: Beef naturally contains creatine, which can help improve strength and endurance.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excess saturated fat may raise cholesterol levels if consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Ribeye is calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef can harbor pathogens such as E. coli. Cook to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C (145 °F).

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ribeye is best cooked over high heat—grill, cast‑iron skillet, or broiler. Let the steak sit at room temperature for about 30 minutes before cooking. Season simply with salt, freshly ground black pepper, butter, or a herb sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh ribeye in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C; thaw in the fridge for 24‑48 hours. Protect from air to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Red Bull sugar‑free energy drink is a zero‑calorie version of the popular stimulant, containing caffeine, taurine, B‑vitamins and flavorings. It is designed to boost alertness and concentration without added sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Red Bull was first launched in Austria in 1987.
The sugar‑free variant appeared in 2008 and quickly gained fans who watch their calorie intake.
One 250 ml can contains about 80 mg of caffeine – roughly the amount in a shot of espresso.
Taurine, a natural amino‑acid, supports heart and muscle function.
Red Bull sponsors numerous extreme sports events worldwide.

items.title: Increased energy and focus
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving alertness and reaction time.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: B‑vitamins (B6, B12, niacin, pyridoxine) help convert food into usable energy.

items.title: Enhanced physical endurance
items.content: Taurine may aid more efficient oxygen utilization by muscles during exercise.

items.title: No sugar
items.content: Provides an energy boost without raising blood glucose levels.

items.title: Low calorie count
items.content: Approximately 5 kcal per can, making it suitable for diet plans.

items.title: Excessive caffeine intake
items.content: High doses can cause anxiety, insomnia, and rapid heart rate.

items.title: Not recommended for children and adolescents
items.content: The high caffeine and taurine content may affect developing nervous systems.

items.title: Interaction with alcohol
items.content: Mixing energy drinks with alcohol increases the risk of dehydration and overexertion.

items.title: Pregnancy and lactation
items.content: Pregnant or nursing women should limit consumption due to caffeine.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Rarely, individuals may react to flavorings or preservatives.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Consume one 250 ml can 30‑60 minutes before mental or physical activity. Do not exceed 2‑3 cans per day. Avoid drinking on an empty stomach if you have a sensitive stomach.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: The frozen yogurt cone with vanilla flavor is a crisp waffle cone filled with smooth, frozen yogurt flavored with natural vanilla. It combines the light tang of yogurt with the sweet aroma of vanilla for a refreshing dessert.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The yogurt is flash‑frozen after filling, preserving most of its probiotic cultures.
Vanilla flavor is derived from natural vanilla bean extract, not artificial aromatics.
The waffle cone is made from whole‑grain flour, adding a bit of nutritional value.
It is a popular summer snack in cafés and cinemas as a lighter alternative to ice cream.
Frozen yogurt typically contains less sugar than traditional ice cream while offering a similarly creamy texture.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Yogurt provides live bacterial cultures that support a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with regular ice cream, frozen yogurt usually has less saturated fat.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Yogurt is a good source of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Vitamin B12
items.content: Yogurt supplies a modest amount of vitamin B12, important for nervous system function.

items.title: Natural vanilla aroma
items.content: Vanilla contains antioxidants such as vanillin, which may have anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Yogurt contains lactose, so people with intolerance should choose lactose‑free versions.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to dairy should avoid this product.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some varieties add sugar; those monitoring blood glucose should check the label.

items.title: Cold dessert
items.content: Eating it straight from the freezer may cause discomfort for people with sensitive teeth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Consume the cone immediately after removing it from the freezer, allowing the yogurt to soften slightly. It can be topped with fresh berries, nuts, or honey for added flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a freezer at –18°C in the original packaging. Once opened, eat within 24 hours to maintain texture and taste.

fruit-salad-excluding-citrus-fruits-with.title: Fruit Salad without Citrus with Non‑Dairy Whipped Topping

content.title: About
content.content: This fruit salad excludes citrus fruits and combines fresh apples, pears, bananas, kiwi, grapes, and strawberries, tossed with a non‑dairy whipped topping (item 4058). The topping is made from plant‑based oils and stabilizers, contains no dairy, and is suitable for vegans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The salad is a popular chilled dish in summer cafés and bistros.
The non‑dairy topping may be based on coconut milk, soy protein, or oat emulsifiers.
The contrast of sweet fruit and light airy topping makes it a hit with children.
For extra flavor, mint, a splash of lime juice (without zest) or a drizzle of honey are sometimes added.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: The fruit mix provides vitamin C, vitamin A, folate, and antioxidants that support immune function.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Apples, pears, and berries supply both soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The plant‑based topping is typically made with oils high in unsaturated fatty acids.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: Many of the fruits have high water content, helping maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Vegan‑friendly
items.content: Absence of dairy ingredients makes the dish safe for those following a vegan diet.

items.title: Allergy to plant ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may react to soy or coconut components in the topping.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Naturally sweet fruits can raise blood sugar; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Risk of spoilage
items.content: Improper storage of fresh fruit can lead to bacterial growth; keep the salad refrigerated.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled; add a dollop of extra topping just before serving. It pairs well with fresh mint, nuts (if no allergy), or a sprinkle of granola.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. The topping may separate; gently stir before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Lettuce (Lactuca sativa) is a leafy vegetable cultivated worldwide. Raw lettuce has a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a crisp texture. It is used in fresh salads, sandwiches, side dishes, and as a base for mixed greens.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lettuce belongs to the Asteraceae family and is a close relative of endive and romaine.
There are over 100 lettuce varieties, differing in leaf shape, color, and texture.
Lettuce was domesticated in ancient Egypt more than 4,000 years ago.
Lettuce leaves are composed of more than 95 % water, making it a very low‑calorie food.
Raw lettuce is rich in vitamin K, which is important for blood clotting.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K plays a key role in blood clotting and supports bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, supports vision and immunity.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially beneficial for pregnant women.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety without adding many calories.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Lettuce provides lutein and zeaxanthin, which protect the eyes from oxidative stress.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw leafy greens can be contaminated with Salmonella or E. coli; thorough washing before consumption is recommended.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may experience oral itching or swelling as an allergy to lettuce.

items.title: Thyroid concerns
items.content: Large amounts of raw lettuce contain glucosinolates, which in excess may affect thyroid function.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat lettuce fresh in salads, as leaf wraps, added to sandwiches, blended into smoothies, or use it as a base for mixed greens. A light squeeze of lemon juice can help preserve its bright color.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store lettuce in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a paper towel and placed in a sealed bag. Properly stored, it stays fresh for 5‑7 days. Remove any wilted leaves to extend shelf life.

content.title: About
content.content: Pastrami is a smoked‑cured meat traditionally made from beef, but it can be produced from any kind of meat (turkey, pork, venison). The reduced‑fat version uses lean cuts and limits added fats, keeping the characteristic smoky flavor and tender texture while lowering the overall fat content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “pastrami” comes from the Hebrew “pastruma,” meaning “dried meat.”
Traditional recipes involve brining with salt, sugar, spices, and nitrites, followed by drying and cold smoking.
Fat reduction is achieved by selecting lean muscle and trimming visible fat before the cure.
Pastrami is often served thinly sliced in sandwiches, but it also appears in salads and hot dishes.
In the United States, pastrami is a staple of Jewish delicatessen cuisine.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Lean pastrami provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Reduced fat content
items.content: Lower fat makes it suitable for calorie‑controlled or low‑saturated‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat used in pastrami supplies heme iron, which helps prevent anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pastrami contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc in pastrami contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: The curing brine gives pastrami a high sodium level, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Nitrites and nitrates
items.content: Traditional curing uses nitrites to preserve color and inhibit bacterial growth; excess intake can be a concern.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergy or intolerance to specific types of meat.

items.title: Caloric density in large portions
items.content: Even with reduced fat, pastrami remains calorie‑dense; overeating can lead to excess energy intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pastrami is typically sliced thin and used in sandwiches, salads, wraps, or as a snack. It can be gently warmed in a pan or microwave to enhance aroma. Pair with mustard, pickles, or whole‑grain bread for a classic experience.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pastrami in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. It stays fresh for about 2 weeks after opening. For longer storage, freeze in a vacuum‑sealed bag for up to 3 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration; discard if it smells sour or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potatoes served in school cafeterias are made from boiled potatoes, butter, and milk or cream. They have a smooth, creamy texture and a mild, slightly sweet flavor that appeals to children.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes are the fourth most produced food crop worldwide after rice, wheat, and corn.
Typical school mashed potatoes are often fortified with vitamins A and D and iron to meet children's daily needs.
In the United States, over 90 % of school lunches include potatoes in the form of mash, fries, or casseroles.
Mashed potatoes are easily digestible and provide quick energy thanks to their high starch content.
In some countries (e.g., Japan) seaweed is added to the mash to boost iodine levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The starch in potatoes supplies a steady release of energy, which is important for active schoolchildren.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and enhances iron absorption from plant foods.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Provides vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When butter is added in moderation, mashed potatoes remain a relatively low‑fat dish suitable for a balanced diet.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: School kitchens sometimes add too much salt; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: If milk or butter is used, children with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein allergy may react.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high glycemic index, so large portions can cause rapid spikes in blood sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the mash hot, either as a standalone side or alongside meat, fish, or vegetables. A sprinkle of fresh herbs (parsley, dill) adds flavor and extra nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared mashed potatoes refrigerated at +2–+4 °C for no more than 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in airtight containers for up to 3 months. Reheat to at least +60 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Queso Asadero is a semi‑hard Mexican cheese made from cow’s milk. It has a mild, slightly buttery flavor and a characteristic stretchiness, which makes it ideal for melting in hot dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the Spanish word “asado,” meaning “roasted” or “baked.”
Traditionally produced in the Mexican states of México and Jalisco, where the climate favors its aging.
Commonly used in classic dishes such as chilaquiles, enchiladas, and fajitas.
Its high meltability often makes it a substitute for mozzarella in recipes requiring a stretchy cheese.
Unlike cheddar, Asadero is not aged for long periods, preserving its gentle taste.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Queso Asadero provides a good amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The cheese supplies high‑quality animal protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains riboflavin (B2) and vitamin B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Phosphorus and zinc
items.content: These minerals help maintain a healthy immune system and metabolic functions.

items.title: Reduced lactose
items.content: During aging part of the lactose is broken down, making the cheese more tolerable for people with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to casein or whey proteins may experience reactions when consuming the cheese.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The cheese is salty, so those with hypertension should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Queso Asadero is calorie‑dense; excessive intake can contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Its saturated fat content calls for moderate consumption, especially for people with heart disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Queso Asadero is often sliced and used in hot dishes: melted in tortillas, added to soups, casseroles, and pizza. It can also be enjoyed fresh, cubed in salads, or served with fruit and nuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cheese in the refrigerator, wrapped in parchment paper or a dedicated cheese film, inside a separate container. Properly stored, it stays fresh for 2–3 weeks. Discard if mold develops or it develops an off‑odor.

yat-ga-mein-with-meat-fish-or-poultry.title: Yat Ga Mein with Meat, Fish, or Poultry

content.title: About
content.content: Yat Ga Mein is a classic Chinese stir‑fried noodle dish made with soy‑based sauce, vegetables and a choice of protein – beef, pork, chicken, duck or fish. It features a savory‑sweet sauce, tender noodles and crisp vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Yat Ga Mein is a popular street‑food item across China and Southeast Asia.
The name comes from Cantonese “Yat Ga” (一加) meaning “one plus”, referring to the optional addition of any meat.
Traditional recipes use egg noodles, though rice or wheat noodles are sometimes substituted.
A fried egg is often placed on top for extra richness.
The sauce is typically made from soy sauce, oyster sauce, a touch of sugar and sesame oil.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Choosing meat, fish or poultry provides complete protein essential for muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Iron source
items.content: Red meats and organ meats commonly used in the dish are good sources of iron, supporting healthy blood.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies B1, B2, B6 and B12 vitamins that aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Added vegetables such as onions, carrots and peppers increase dietary fiber, promoting digestion.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: Despite a mildly sweet sauce, the overall sugar content remains modest.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy and oyster sauces are salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Soy sauce can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Fatty meat cuts
items.content: Using fattier cuts of pork or beef raises calories and saturated fat levels.

items.title: Potential fish toxins
items.content: When fish is used, ensure it is fresh to avoid food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, straight from the wok. Garnish with fresh cilantro, lime wedges, or sliced chili for extra flavor. Optional toppings include a fried egg, toasted sesame seeds or cucumber ribbons.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed within 2–3 hours of cooking. Leftovers should be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator and consumed within 24 hours, reheating quickly in a pan or microwave.
